# Planning a small exhibition

An exhibition begins with a question. What should a visitor notice, understand, or remember after leaving the room? A collection of interesting objects can still feel confusing if the connection between them is unclear. Write the question on a sheet of paper and keep it nearby while choosing the exhibits.

Start with a rough plan of the room. Mark entrances, windows, power sockets, and any area that must remain clear. Then place a few large objects on the plan before adding smaller ones. This helps reveal problems that are easy to miss in a list, such as a display case blocking the view from the doorway.

Labels need a similar kind of planning. Give each one a clear purpose. A heading can introduce a subject; a short paragraph can explain why an object matters; a caption can identify the maker and date. Visitors should be able to choose how much they read. They should also be able to understand the main idea without reading every word.

Ask someone who has not worked on the exhibition to walk through the draft layout. Watch where they stop and which questions they ask. Their comments may reveal missing information, but silence can be useful evidence too. A label that nobody notices may need a different position or a stronger opening sentence.

Finally, leave time to check the details. Confirm names and dates against the collection record, test any audio equipment, and view the labels from a seated position. Good access depends on many small decisions. Review those decisions with people who have different needs and make changes while there is still time to do so.
